question.worked_solution:
First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡\theta -{sinh}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

Setting $\theta =2x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{cosh}^{2}⁡(2x)-{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x) & =1 \\ 1+{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x) & ={cosh}^{2}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2+2{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2(1+{sinh}^{2}⁡(2x))}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2{cosh}^{2}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)+C\end{aligned}
$$
